This work introduces MG-GLAM, software specifically designed to generate full-scale cosmological $N$-body simulations within a wide range of modified gravity (MG) frameworks at remarkable speed. We detail the code's implementation, validation through numerical tests, and initial outcomes from extensive suite of simulations applying three major classes of MG models characterized by conformal coupling, including the $f(R)$ gravity framework, symmetron, and coupled quintessence scenarios. Adapted from GLAM (a concurrent particle-mesh solver), MG-GLAM leverages a high-performance multigrid relaxation approach capable of resolving the distinct nonlinear partial differential equations defining these models. Regarding $f(R)$ gravity, our code has been extended to cover various signatures both degenerate and non-degenerate, alongside the integration of symmetron and conformally coupled MG models. Verified via comparisons to both individual particle simulations and analytical approximations, the Suite of simulations package generates realizations of these systems with unique statistical properties. Compared to existing standard $N$-body codes for point particles, MG-GLAM demonstrates an impressive acceleration factor, generating simulations in these additional models roughly ten times faster. Additionally, the code facilitates the creation of MG-specific realizations of dark matter halos and matter power spectra. These capabilities are well-suited to support ongoing and future experimental efforts, which require the generation of massive numerical realizations to calibrate next-generation cosmological surveys.

This investigation conducts a linear analysis of a turbulent, methane-fuelled, atmospheric jet to forecast how the flow reacts to upstream acoustic actuation. Capturing heat release variations is essential for understanding thermoacoustic instabilities and flame acoustic signatures within a linear theory. Distinct from prior research, this work employs active combustion theories to integrate flame heat release oscillations triggered by acoustic signals, requiring that the combustion model be linearized. Although linearizing Large Eddy Simulation (LES) and Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) models introduces closure issues, rendering their application problematic in this context, Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) models effectively avoid these difficulties and emerge as appropriate choices outside of linearity constraints. Consequently, a Wilcox $k$-$\omega$ turbulence model is utilized to simulate mean characteristics, while its linearized forms represent perturbation fields. Two leading combustion models—the Markstein and Arrhenius models—are adjusted using RANS-derived mean values and the jet's inherent acoustic mode, eliminating the need for extensive flame experiments. Linear theory, combined with these calibrated models, successfully predicts acoustic receptivity, accurately reflecting both flame light emission intensity and temperature distribution oscillations when compared against high-fidelity LES and experimental data.

The detection in the Galactic Centre region of X-ray source variants that exhibit no detectable outbursts despite over a decade of scrutiny has fueled the hypothesis that numerous stellar-mass black holes inhabit this area. A foundational premise of the argument that such accretion events signify black holes is the assumption that low mass X-ray binary (LMXB) systems containing neutron星星 (NSs) cannot possess long intervals between outburst transients. We demonstrate herein, however, that approximately half of the recognized transient NS-BH-2 systems already possess recorded recurrence times exceeding one decade, thereby invalidating the claim that the lack of nearby BH systems with long quiescence is evidence for a population of unassociated BHs. Furthermore, we propose that transient NS-BH-2 systems exhibit variable outburst timescales governed either by intrinsic differences among the systems or observational biases; consequently, the presence of persistent sources in the Galactic Centre is better explained as quiescent X-ray binaries (mostly NS-2 systems) whose activity falls below detection thresholds due to extended quiescence times unrelated to the presence of black holes.

Bipartite graphs illustrate the connections between two non-overlapping groups of entities and are frequently depicted with a two-level arrangement. In this representation, each group occupies a parallel horizontal row, containing vertices where vertices from distinct levels interact through edges curving between the rows. A prevalent optimization goal within these visualizations is to minimize edge crossings, an objective that is resource-intensive and can still yield cluttered diagrams impairing legibility. This study examines a recent technique that eliminates crossings by dividing vertices, specifically aiming to calculate the least amount of vertex splitting required to achieve planarity. The research establishes that deciding if a drawing can achieve planarity after splitting no more than $k$ vertices constitutes an algorithm with fixed-parameter tractability with respect to $k$.

This paper outlines our approach to designing feedback mechanisms for thruster-augmented walking robots. Assuming the supervisory controller is sufficiently calibrated, we focus solely on adjusting joint trajectory setpoints. We introduce a reference-governor-based intermediate filter that ensures adherence to required performance constraints. Since model modifications or impacts disrupt desired periodic orbits, we ensure hybrid invariance through robust predictive schemes applied within a brief window of the gait cycle; we uniquely employ our robot's thrusters to achieve this invariibility. The primary advantage of our method, compared to existing nonlinear control algorithms based on optimization, is that guaranteed satisfaction of single support phase constraints does not depend on costly numeric computations. Moreover, the proposed control framework for thruster-assisting gaits innovatively permits the targeted use of robustness and performance enhancements throughout the gait sequence, a novelty unrecorded in the current literature.

Developing numerical schemes for time-dependent partial differential equations often requires them to maintain essential features of the continuous solution, such as conservation laws or other geometric attributes. A substantial legacy exists in the study of discretization schemes that preserve such structures, encompassing both theoretical validations of standard methods and innovative designs offering both high-order precision and exact preservation. However, when integrated with implicit tanning steps, these methods carry a significant drawback: maintaining structure preservation typically demands the exact solution of the discrete system at each time-step. While this constraint is manageable for small systems, it becomes infeasible for the extensive linear systems generated by standard spatial-temporal PDE discretization for larger scales. This paper introduces a modification to the flexible generalized minimum residual (FGMRES) algorithm that imposes specific constraints on approximate solutions. The proposed approach is applied to both conservation and dissipative system scenarios.

Non-rigid registration stands as a fundamental technique in soft-tissue navigation, specifically within laparoscopic liver surgery. Additionally, aligning pre-operative and intra-operative data poses a significant hurdle; this is largely because liver tissues typically possess few distinct surface markers while the imaging methods employ vastly different, specific types of noise mitigation strategies. This paper describes the training of a convolutional neural network capable of simultaneously identifying surface correspondences alongside non-rigid registration. Uniquely, the model is trained upon physically rigorous biomechanical simulations involving deforming structures of organ-like shapes with various generated configurations, granting it the capacity to generalize instantly to specific patient organs without requiring retraining. By incorporating synthetic noise into intra-operative surface data during the training phase, the system achieves robustness against imperfect surgical image quality. Upon execution, the model outputs a displacement field that accurately maps a full, pre-operative three-volume onto the fragmented intra-operative surface. Experimental results demonstrate strong adaptability when applied to real-world scenarios and sustained a high inference speed, and the accompanying source code has been made publicly accessible.

A graph $G$ exhibits the Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian (PMH) property if every one of its perfect matchings can be paired with another perfect matching such that their union forms a Hamiltonian cycle. Research into graphs satisfying this condition, which began in the 1970s through the work of Las Vergnas and Häggkvist, explores the intersections of edge colourings, matchings, and Hamiltonicity. Our study focuses on cubic graphs to characterize those where every perfect matching is a valid colour in a proper 3-edge-colouring. We demonstrate the equivalence between this condition and the graphs being even-2-factorable (E2F), defined as graphs in which all 2-factors consist exclusively of even-length cycles. Because the scenario for bipartite cubic graphs is trivial as they inherently satisfy E2F, we restrict our investigation to non-bipartite cubic graphs. It is established that possessing the PMH-property provides a sufficient condition for a graph to be E2F, though it is neither necessary. Our specific contribution is the construction of an infinite family of distinct E2F, non-bipartite cubic graphs, parameterized by a pair of positive integers $(p,q)$, which are not assumed to have the PMH-property despite being even 2-factorized.

By leveraging the significant role play calls in software functionality, our method provides secure execution by rejecting superfluous calls while maintaining compatibility with legal operations, such as those within loops, which existing solutions struggle to validate. Evaluations across three widely used microservices confirm that Timeloops successfully learns system call filters that reject 9,000+ unique malicious configurations while rejecting none of the permitted calls; furthermore, our automatically generated filters demonstrate superior rejection of 10 well-known container escape attacks compared to those produced by existing methods.

In this study, we recast heart sound classification as an image-based task and employ a two-dimensional Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) utilizing a VGG-Style architecture. The Log-Mel spectrograms of input cardiac sounds are divided into fixed segments, which are subsequently processed through consecutive convolutional layers, fully connected layers, and softmax output units. Notably, our model requires no data normalization, data augmentation, or manual feature extraction. Extensive experiments on an auditory dataset containing 4,620 noisy records—comprising four cardiac categories: murmurs, rupture, normal, and stenosis—across multiple noisy environments demonstrate high performance with a weighted accuracy of 97.04%. These promising outcomes suggest the method's feasibility for deploying noisy cardiac diagnosis systems in real-world medical scenarios.

The swift advancement of computing technology has enabled wearable devices, such as wristbands and mobile phones, to easily gather personal health data on activities, fitness, and sleep. Smart healthcare leverages machine learning models trained on vast amounts of this user data to achieve significant progress. Nevertheless, two major obstacles remain primary hurdles. First, user data is often stored in fragmented 'silos,' complicating data aggregation while maintaining strong privacy safeguards; this is known as non-identifiable distribution. Secondly, those medical models developed on the cloud do not perform reliably on personalized use-cases, a challenge hereafter termed as heterogeneity of devices. Federating on the user side in this research has two crucial advantages: first, it avoids the need for data transmission and thus offers a mechanism to ensure data security and privacy, and the other advantage lies that each model can be improved according to its respective use and thus becomes personalized to individual users without losing accuracy for general health services including monitoring of activity and disease. Our approach, called 'FedHealth,' is the first 'transfer federated learning' design to handle the requirements of real-life wearable health scenarios. It runs two major steps in sequence using federated learning and transfer learning for aggregating data and finally establishing a customized model tailored for the user's specifics and needs. Our experiments show that it offers better performance than current methods.

A primary issue remains the tendency of reinforcement learning models to generalize poorly to new tasks lying outside their training data distributions; consequently, continual learning algorithms have garnered considerable attention. Beyond developing such algorithmic methods, there is an urgent need for structured challenge environments, tailored experiments, and evaluation metrics to gauge research advancements. We meet this gap by introducing Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a novel Unity-based, first-person 3D exploration framework that allows for continuous realignment to produce various task structures and their variants, alongside intricate, evolving evaluation curricula. Unlike worlds generated purely by random procedures, our method establishes a systematic curriculum design based on deliberate changes supported by specific metrics to evaluate transferability, performance recovery rates, and data usage efficiency. Collectively, combining L2Explorer with our evaluation methodology offers a comprehensive framework for advancing future research in open-world settings. This system is specifically capable of rigorously benchmarking lifelong learning strategies.

Rapidly circulating through social media on a global scale, fake news threatens users and entire communities, especially as it emerges with alarming speed. While deep learning models excel when trained extensively on data for specific events, their effectiveness often declines due to domain shifts when encountering new topics. Consequently, current detection methods face major obstacles when dealing with emergent fake news events, where accumulating large, well-annotated datasets is impractical. Furthermore, integrating knowledge about new events currently necessitates retraining models or continuous fine-tuning—a process that is often costly, inefficient, and unfeasible in real-world applications.

To solve these issues, this paper presents MetaFEND, an end-to-end framework capable of learning to identify fake news from newly emerged events using limited verified data (few-shot setting). The model combines meta-learning techniques with neural process methodologies to maximize performance. Key innovations include a proposed label embedding module for processing categorical nuances and a hard attention mechanism to filter out irrelevant content to enhance detection efficacy. Rigorous testing on multimedia datasets sourced from Twitter and Weibo demonstrates that MetaFEND effectively identifies misinformation on unseen events and surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods.

Quantum tunneling, a process without classical correspondence that can compete with Coulomb interactions to generate complex behavior, serves as a focal topic. Silicon doped with phosphorus allows researchers to position atoms with precision and investigate the regimes resulting from this competition. However, current systems rely on wavefunctions tied to crystal band symmetries, creating inherent sensitivity to tunneling effects. This study employs scanning tunneling microscopy to directly visualize lattice-aperiodic valley interference between connected atoms in silicon. Our atomistic analysis details how envelope anisotropy, valley interference influences, and dopant arrangement affect the Heisenberg spin exchange interaction. We demonstrate that exchange can be made resilient to valley interference by strategic engineering of dopant placement along certain planar crystallographic orientations, resulting in behavior analogous to a vacuum state. In this regime, maximum exchange occurs at donor orbital overlap, with pair-to-consist variations restricted to under a factor of 10 despite precise positioning limitations. This stability persists across extended distances, covering both the high-fidelity quantum computation regime dominated by strong Coulomb interaction and the strongly coupled donor arrays essential for simulation in silicon.

Model selection or sparse modelling for categorical variables remains problematic, even with a moderate variable count, as encoding each category requires a parameter, quickly leading to non-solutions. Although Group Lasso is an established and efficient tool for selecting continuous or categorical variables, its estimates for individual levels of selected factors are rarely identical. Because of the lack uniformity, resulting models often fail to achieve true sparsity, hindering interpretability. We address this by proposing a two-stage strategy: initially, dimensionality is reduced using Group Lasso; subsequently, final selection is made over a narrowed candidate space via an information criterion applied to clusters of factor levels constructed after the initial selection phase. We examine algorithm accuracy within sparse, high-dimensional contexts, applying our approach to both synthetic examples and realistic datasets, demonstrating that our methods generally outperform current-state-of-the-art algorithms regarding prediction accuracy or model size efficiency at the variable dimension.

Nanometer-thick rare-earth-transition metal (RE-TM) alloys, characterized by their precisely engineered compositions and robust out-of-plane magnetic anisotropy, are currently the subject of intense research for applications involving ultrafast magnetophotonics. However, simultaneously achieving the lateral nanosizing essential for device miniaturization and retaining tunable optomagnetic performance along with preserved magnetic anisotropy remains a significant challenge. In this work, we embed nanoscale Tb$_{18}$Co$_{82}$ ferrimagnetic particles—including strong out-of-plane magnetic anisotropy—with gold plasmonic nanoantennas. This integration constructs micron-scale magnetophotonic crystals that produce sharp and narrow magneto-optical resonances, which can be precisely manipulated by both external magnetic fields and the incidence direction of incident light. The resulting narrow Fano-type resonance is generated by the coupling between inter-element surface plasmons of individual antennae and the Rayleigh anomalies of the collective antenna array; a computational framework grounded in Maxwell theory provides a complete explanation for this optical and magneto-optical mechanism. Ultimately, this stable magnetophotonic crystal establishes a platform for developing novel, high-symmetry optical directionality sensors and creating foundational structures for all-optical magnetization switching in ferrimagnetic RE-TM systems assisted by plasmonics.

Knowledge distillation serves as a proven strategy for expediting deep neural networks, wherein a smaller "student" model mimics the soft probability outputs of a large "teacher" network. Traditionally, this process requires access to both the input training data and the internal parameters of the white-box teacher transfer; however, constraints such as storage limits or privacy concerns in practical deployments often make these prerequisites unattainable. This work introduces Decision-based Black-Box (DB3) knowledge distillation, a technique that trains a student model by extracting knowledge exclusively from a teacher where parameters are inaccessible and decisions are revealed only as final class labels, without softmax probabilities. Initially, we address settings where training data remains available: we estimate a sample's robustness by measuring its distance to the teacher's decision boundaries, utilizing these metrics to generate soft labels for standard distillation. Furthermore, we address the more demanding case wherein even training data access is blocked by proposing a transfer dataset constructed from synthetic samples that are maximally distinguished by the teacher; these samples receive generated soft labels to facilitate training. Evaluations across multiple datasets and networks validate the efficacy of these methods. Source code can be obtained at https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd/.

Chances like attending college can boost upward mobility, allowing people to reach socioeconomic levels higher than their parents achieved. In 2015, the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC) implemented a novel luminosity scanning technique known as "Emittance Scans." This approach facilitated emittance and closed orbit assessments at the single-beam granularity. By precisely determining variations in closed orbit caused by beam-beam interactions, researchers were able to directly measure, quantitatively establish, and substantiate long-range PACMAN effect phenomena, with results closely aligning those generated by enhanced numerical simulations in the TRAIN code suite.

This study addresses a distributed optimization challenge in multi-agent systems where a subset of nodes behave maliciously. Specifically, these adversaries attempt to drive the network off the optimal trajectory by corrupting data transmitted to their neighbors and imposing high bandwidth costs through excessive communication. Accordingly, we introduce a quantized, distributed gradient-based algorithm designed for benign agents. This section establishes the convergence of the proposed method to a vicinity of the global optimal solution, analytizing performance under both bandwidth constraints and adversarial interference. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings with numerical simulations.

Detecting fluctuations in the cosmic microwave background (CMB), often called anisotropies, is among the most vital techniques in cosmological research. Due to the faintness of this signal, scientists have built ever more sophisticated and sensitive instruments capable of scanning the sky across multiple frequencies with thousands of detectors sensitive to polarization. As these experiments reach higher levels of sensitivity, instrumental artifacts are often becoming the primary obstacle to fully realizing their data potential. We introduce *s4cmb* (Systematics for CMB), a Python toolkit designed to generate raw, bolometric-based time-domain data streams for current-generation CMB missions while realistically inserting instrumental systematic effects. *s4cmb* aims not only to evaluate the impact of such systematics on actual datasets and to inform the architecture of future detectors but also to create more authentic simulations essential for refining analytical methodologies.

Word reordering represents a language generation challenge where models must arrange unordered inputs into coherent text using ordered output, based primarily on existing research employing standard models or neural networks. Despite this history, researchers have not yet investigated the benefits of large, word-oriented language models or proposed reasons why pre-trained ones succeed in these scenarios. In our work with the BART model, both its effectiveness in solving this word ordering challenge as well as partial sorting are demonstrated and compared. In addition, probing methods were utilized to explore how success might explain performance. The results revealed one key explanation: how pre-trained syntactical dependency patterns help BART perform word reorientation. Finally, partial sorting of linear texts with BART produces improved performance that complements and strengthens these findings.

The swift evolution in generating and distributing ultra-realistic media across social networks necessitates the immediate development of broadly applicable deepfake detection solutions. Observing that existing deep learning-based fake generators and discriminators often rely on recurrent network structures like Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with their inherent temporal dependencies, we infer that artificial features in the frequency domain should effectively identify deepfake forgeries. Furthermore, given that deepfake attacks manifest diverse spatial distortions, our proposed method, Multi-Domain Cross-Stitched Network (MD-CSDNetwork), integrates features from multiple domains to enhance performance. Specifically, we construct a model architecture designed to extract and combine features in both spatial and frequency domains from various image subspaces. To implement frequency-domain extraction, the spatial-stitched network employs Gray-Component Continuation (GCC) mapping for transformation between spatial and frequency spaces. Additionally, we develop a frequency-stitched network using Fast Fourier Transformation (FFT) and Reverse Fast Fourier Transformation (RFFT). Evaluation results across three distinct datasets confirm the broad applicability of MD-CSDNetwork and demonstrate that it consistently outperforms current state-of-the-methods on three specific deepfake generation algorithms.

Finally, our validated visible-light framework allows the analysis of future observations, such as upcoming TESS mission spectrum data.

The Jost function method has been adapted within the RPA framework to detect poles in the complex energy plane exhibiting complex RPA eigenvalues. This approach successfully identified poles associated with RPA excited states, specifically locating the electric dipole giants resonances in $^{16}$O. Despite the conventional view of the electric dipole giant resonance in $^{16}$O as a single state with significant strength and width, the results indicate that, under RPA conditions, the resonance comprises multiple poles. Each pole functions as a separate entity with distinctive widths, underlying origins, response characteristics regarding residual interactions, and density fluctuation component structures.

Community detection poses significant challenges yet remains highly relevant across diverse fields, encompassing everything from power grids and atmospheric science to social and financial networks. However, addressing these issues in many dynamic systems is often difficult because the inherent complexity makes deriving traditional mathematical models for clustering impractical. Furthermore, effective clustering of dynamic systems must explicitly consider their temporal behavior. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel methodology for clustering dynamical systems using only raw time-series data, thereby inherently capturing the underlying dynamics. This approach defines a distance or similarity metric between states based on the interdependencies they exert upon one another. For computational implementation, we employ the Koopman operator framework, enabling us to account for system nonlinearities when present. This allows the framework to extend its applicability to a broad spectrum of domains. We demonstrate the approach's validity by applying it to three distinct systems: as a baseline proof of concept a linear system, and as real-world examples the highly nonlinear IEEE 39 bus power network and atmospheric variables observed across the Amazon rainforest.

Implementing neural text generation models via Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) presents significant challenges due to the non-differentiability of the full training loop, a limitation existing approaches address poorly with either inaccurate gradient estimates or poor-quality sentence embeddings. Drawing inspiration from sparse coding, we introduce SparseGAN to feed sparse, semantically meaningful sentence representations to the discriminator. This is achieved by treating the embedding matrix as an over-complete dictionary, approximating generator output features at each timestep through a linear combination of only a few selected word embeddings. These robust semantic representations streamline adversarial learning and ensure full differentiability, while empirical results across multiple datasets demonstrate performance gains, particularly improving BLEU scores for whole sequences.

The concept that life can migrate across planetary systems, known as interstellar panspermia, dates back decades but remains hard to validate through observation. To evaluate the chances of confirming this phenomenon, we established a mathematical framework accounting for factors such as the lifespan of resilient microbes in transit, the dispersion of stellar velocities, and the distribution of ejected material. Our results indicate that the statistical pair distribution of inhabited planetary systems can effectively detect interstellar transfer of life under the specific condition that ejecta move with sufficient divergence relative to stellar motions. By offering heuristic estimates of key parameters in different astrophysical contexts, we conclude that open and globular clusters are the most suitable regions for testing this hypothesis.

A core focus of animal populations research is understanding how space is used and how resources are selected, a topic often addressed through telemetry data and resource selection functions (RSF). Wildlife research also heavily emphasizes estimating and modeling population density and size; recent advancements in spatial capture-recapture (SCR) models facilitate this by analyzing individual encounter histories alongside auxiliary capture location data. While SCR models contain encounter probability functions that resemble RSFs, there was historically a gap in extending these models for explicit joint inference on space use and resource selection. We introduce a statistical framework for these objectives that merges SCR data—such as that generated by mist-nets, trap-catch, or camera traps—with spatial resource usage data from telemetry-tagged individuals utilizing marginal likelihood methods to simultaneously estimate SCR and RSF model parameters. Our methodology demonstrates increased precision for estimating both population density and the parameters of standard SCR models. Furthermore, we identify that while SCR data can sufficiently estimate RSF parameters for analyzing space usage, accuracy improves significantly when telemetry data are integrated. Critically, we find that conventional SCR models using symmetric, stationary encounter probability functions tend to yield density bias when space use varies with landscape characteristics. Consequently, when estimating density using capture-recapture, it is essential to account for spatial usage patterns wherever feasible.

Multilayer networks represent a valuable tool for modeling and analyzing the dynamical properties of diverse systems. While providing a more realistic depiction with richer complexity compared to single-layer models, they inherently introduce analytical difficulties. This work presents an approach to study Kuramoto oscillators on multilayer networks by constructing an "inverted" join of the matrices associated with inter-and intra-layer connectivity. This yields a simplified, equivalent representation of the full system dynamics, from whose solutions we derive results directly applicable to the original multi-layer context. Furthermore, this framework allows for the investigation of states' stability: by examining the Jacobian of the reduced model, we infer properties about the Jacobian of the composite multilayer structure. Unlike previous assumptions, this strategy is adaptable regardless of the specific wiring patterns between nodes within a layer. Overall, these findings suggest that adopting such simplified, equivalent frameworks offers more tractable methods to understand dynamics, thereby advancing the comprehension of multilayer network behaviors.

Accurate traffic control depends on effectively estimating traffic states. This research proposes an integrative, nonparametric technique for short-term queue length estimation, utilizing partial queue observations on a cycle-by-cycle basis collected from probe vehicles. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on random arrival assumptions or the need for primary parameter calibration, this method employs straightforward algebraic formulations contingent solely on signal timing. Specifically, for a given approach lane, conditional queue lengths are modeled using a Negative Hypergeometric distribution based on probe location, counts, timestamp, and time intervals (such as signal phase termination). Field test data comparing these nonparametric estimators against both parametric models and standard Highway Capacity Manual methods demonstrates that the new technique achieves parity in accuracy when estimating queue lengths.

Numerical relativity simulations involving non-trivial matter configurations require solving the ADM Hamiltonian and momentum constraints to determine initial metric data. This study introduces a novel method grounded in the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless (CTT) decomposition. Rather than treating mean curvature ($K$) as a fixed value and solving the Hamiltonian constraint as a second-order elliptic equation, this new scheme involves selecting a specific conformal factor to derive $K$ via an algebraic equation within a iterative multigrid framework—effectively rendering the Hamiltonian constraint irrelevant. Investigated using spherical simulations, this Hamiltonian-constraint-free methodology proves to be more efficient than traditional CTT strategies while successfully resolving previously problematic spherical scenarios involving previously difficult initial conditions.

The resurgence in research regarding magnetic materials that display a significant anomalous Hall effect despite negligible magnetization stems from the desire to control and understand these phenomena. Antiferromagnetic materials within the antiperovskite structure are a developing class unique for diverse properties derived from their intricate electronic bands and magnetic arrangements; nonetheless, reports quantifying the anomalous Nernst effect in this group remain scarce. This limitation is partially attributed to the difficulty in accurately extracting the anomalous Nernst coefficient through experiments. Addressing this, we present new experimental findings on the anomalous Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN antiferromagnetic antiperovkslite thin films. By utilizing the same sample and geometry for both Hall and Nernst measurements, we achieve a direct comparison of the effects and calculate specific coefficients for the anomalous Nernst response and conductivity in Mn$_3$NiN. Furthermore, by meticulously evaluating the thermal gradient across the sample and validating findings with finite element modeling, we substantiate the reliability of the primary results.

Imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy are essential for researching and identifying novel functional materials. Modern advances in automation and experimental methods allow these techniques to execute measurements rapidly and with greater precision, thereby generating extensive datasets. These technological leaps are most evident within synchrotron light sources. Consequently, machine learning (ML) approaches are increasingly utilized to analyze real-time data. nevertheless, conceptual and technical hurdles persist; these include the knowledge gap among general facility users regarding ML, and the complexities of integrating ML models. In this article, we showcase several representative ML strategies tailored for on-the-fly analysis across multiple National Synchrotron Light Source-II (NSLS-II) beamlines. We present these instances educatively to facilitate the incorporation of models into current experimental workflows, empowering practitioners to implement similar ML algorithms at NSLS-II or comparable infrastructures. The proposed framework illustrates how diverse ML algorithms and feedback loops can merge effectively into established experiments with minimal effort, leveraging the Bluesky Suite for experimental orchestration and data management.

We challenge ourselves by examining if a parallel exists between brain neurons and societal individuals, investigating the prerequisites for individual cognition required to cultivate collective intelligence, and specifically which individual traits contribute most significantly. Drawing on research from population ecology regarding why some groups are intelligent while others are merely collections of individuals, we observe that high-average intelligence is not a solitary prerequisite; a group can achieve greater collective wisdom if its members exhibit moderate intelligence but high variability in skills, while prioritizing information diversity to ensure incoming data remains reliable, relevant, and complementary. Furthermore, contrary to the assumption that larger groups are inherently smarter, we note that group intelligence can actually decline as they expand if members become more similar to one another. This paper investigates the maximum performance improvement achieved by optimal power control compared to binary (on/off) schemes within large interference networks. Leveraging Extremal Network theory and Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) frameworks, it moves beyond numerical GDoF calculations typical of previous work to examine binary power control as a distinct strategy capable of matching optimal control in certain scenarios. The study establishes formal lower and upper bounds for this extremal gain; specifically, it proves the gain is lower-bounded in specific Extremal Networks and upper-bounded universally across all networks. Most significantly, the research demonstrates that the extremal gain grows at a rate of $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ as the user count $K$ increases, indicating that binary power control can achieve near-optimal performance relative to continuous options with significantly fewer active (non-zero power) users.

This paper introduces a Multi-Timestep Solver Algorithm (M-TSA) designed to integrate multiple timescales during particle collisions in simulations involving particle-laden flows with explicit resolution. While current standard methods artificially stretch collision time steps to match several flow solver intervals, such an approach introduces unphysical constraints that negatively impact simulation outcomes, as particles remain sensitive to the artificial stretching. Conversely, the proposed MMA employs distinct time steps to accurately resolve the coupled dynamics of fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions.

Our assessment evaluated this methodology for both particle-wall and particle-particle interactions, identifying an optimal iteration count for substepping that yielded results—using traditional hard-sphere interactions—showing no measurable difference against continuous contact models. Subsequently, the MMA was applied to scale-up simulations combining multiple particle types with interaction potentials ranging from continuous contact through hard-sphere to artificial-dams breakdown, yielding results that did not differ significantly from those obtained via conventional time-expansion models. The primary advantage of the proposed MMA is its ability to accurately resolve physical collisions without incurring the excessive computational burden used by traditional methods, thus reducing total simulation time. As a result, it enables scale-up simulations involving tens or even thousands of particles governed by physical interaction rules.

Quenching and annealing represent opposing approaches to the time-evolution of quantum systems; annealing slowly adjusts a Hamiltonian's parameters to explore equilibrium phases for solving complex optimizations, while quenching imposes sudden changes that create non-equilibrium states. The vertical shear instability (VSI) involves hydrodynamical processes requiring swift gas cooling; it is posited to function in the outer sectors of protoplanetary disks. Although the VSI generates vertical turbulent motions capable of influencing dust accumulation and sinking, dust dynamics can conversely dampen the instability: reduced gas opacity due to dust removal hampers cooling in the already thin outer regions. Utilizing linear analysis, this research quantifies how dust evolution stabilizes the VSI. By devising a cooling timescale model that accounts for dust maturation beyond one micron and size-dependent sedimentation, we integrate it with linear stability analysis to determine VSI activity regions (the "VSI zones") and their peak growth rates at various radii. Results indicate that dust maturation and sinking confine the VSI zone more tightly along the midplane with a narrower radial extent; specifically, at 50 AU within a standard AKARI disk configuration, growth rates diminish by an order of magnitude, the VSI zone shrinks to approximately 30 AU, and turbulence becomes restricted to the lower midlayers compared to scenarios without dust dynamics. These findings imply that dust-driven damping helps regulate outer-region dust evolution and suppresses fluid turbulence.

Individuals involved with the criminal justice system disproportionately experience mental health disorders. Drawing upon data from North Carolina courts covering 1994 to 2009, this study analyzes whether requiring offenders on probation to receive mental healthcare lowers their subsequent likelihood of reincarceration. Measuring atomic disorder levels is vital for understanding how changes in local structural environments influence material performance and longevity. This study utilizes graph neural networks to establish a physically interpretable index for local disorder. This index characterizes the variety of immediate atomic arrangements as a smooth continuum ranging from solid to liquid states, evaluated relative to thermal fluctuations. We demonstrate this new approach across three representative cases with distinct disorder levels: solid-liquid interfaces, polycrystalline microstructures, and grain boundaries. Focusing specifically on aluminum, we illustrate how this method captures the spatiotemporal development of such boundaries, including a rigorous mathematical definition of the boundary separating order and disorder within space. Additionally, we identify physics-consistent gradients emerging from these continuous disorder maps to aid in evaluating and forecasting material behavior and potential failures. Collectively, our framework offers a conceptual and adaptable method for linking complicated local atomic architectures to broader material phenomena.

Knowledge Tracing (KT) applies students' historical interaction records to model their evolving knowledge states and predict their future learning outcomes. While deep learning-based approaches for KT have recently achieved significant advancements, the exact drivers behind these DL-KT models remain elusive, and their proper evaluation and analysis continue to be difficult tasks. Specifically, existing methods typically rely on proprietary and custom data cleaning workflows, impeding experimental standardization. Moreover, these studies often utilize varying protocols that fail to reflect genuine educational environments. To resolve these issues, we present *\textsc{pyKT}*, a robust Python-driven benchmark framework designed to ensure reliable cross-model assessments of DL-KT methods. This library features integrated, standardized data processing pipelines across seven datasets from diverse fields, along with implementations of ten frequently compared DL-KT models for transparent analysis. Insights drawn from our meticulous and rigorous experiments reveal key observations on optimizing DL-KT, including the finding that improper evaluation settings induce label leakage which artificially inflates performance, and that many current DL-KT improvements show negligible progress compared to the seminal DL-KT model introduced by Piech et al. \cite{piech2015deep}. We have made *\textsc{pyKT}* along with our comprehensive empirical results publicly available at https://pykt.org/ and invite contributions from researchers and practitioners alike.
